result:
I've read the full brief. Here are my findings.

```
VERDICT
The three headline fixes are structurally in place for the seat that was burned (Grok), but the escalation fix was never applied to the Cursor seat, which auto-approves MCP servers and has no MCPTool deny — that door is open again the moment a sibling wmw-* seat appears in ~/.cursor/mcp.json. None of the read-only or escalation guarantees are canary-verified: armcheck asserts that the right flags are passed, never that a read-only call actually cannot write or escalate. The canary file is also fragile in ways that let it pass while the rig is unsafe (single-line readline, no crash isolation, no release-path test, no negative write probes), so "ALL ARMED" is closer to a prayer than a proof.

Q1 THE THREE FIXES
  1. injection      HOLDS for the Cursor seat (prompt spilled to a generated file at pkt-glm.md:461-476; only an ASCII-checked generated pointer reaches argv; model id bound by _MODEL_RE at :125; sessionId bound by _UUID_RE at :126). VARIANT MISSED: wmw_gemini_mcp.py:114 still puts the raw caller-controlled prompt on argv (`-p prompt`), and wmw_grok_mcp.py:113/114 puts `-m model` through the weak `_safe_argv` (no metachar rejection, only a no-leading-dash rule). Both are safe only because `agy.exe`/`grok.exe` are native binaries today; if either is ever wrapped in a .cmd shim (the exact shape that burned Cursor), the injection vector reopens on two of three seats.
  2. read-only      HOLDS BY CONSTRUCTION, NOT BY EVIDENCE. Cursor passes `--mode ask --trust` (pkt-glm.md:482), Grok pins deny rules + `--disallowed-tools Agent` + `--permission-mode default` (pkt-glm.md:122-133), Gemini pins `--mode plan` (pkt-glm.md:113). The original bug was "a flag we trusted did not restrict"; the fix swaps flags but no canary proves the new flags actually prevent a write on the current CLI version — armcheck only checks that refusal messages appear for bad arguments, never that a read-only call leaves the filesystem untouched.
  3. escalation     BROKEN. The fix (deny `MCPTool`, `--disallowed-tools Agent`) was applied to wmw_grok_mcp.py only. wmw_cursor_mcp.py:489 passes `--approve-mcps` and has NO MCPTool deny and NO `--disallowed-tools Agent`. The code comment at pkt-glm.md:484-488 admits "this auto-approves whatever is in that file" and the only control is a handwritten warning to keep sibling wmw-* seats out of ~/.cursor/mcp.json. The moment the operator follows the documented plan to "open cursor-codex and cursor-gemini next" (pkt-glm.md:115), a read-only Cursor call can drive those metered seats and spend — the exact 2026-08-23 escalation, re-pointed at the Cursor seat. Gemini has no MCPTool denial either.

Q2 NEW FINDINGS (ranked)

  CRITICAL / wmw_cursor_mcp.py:489 (`--approve-mcps`) / A read-only Cursor call auto-approves every MCP server in ~/.cursor/mcp.json. Pair it with any sibling wmw-* seat (already planned) and it escalates around its own read-only mode and around the council lock, because the sibling spends, not the Cursor seat. / Either drop `--approve-mcps` on read-only calls, or deny `MCPTool` and `Agent` on the Cursor seat exactly as Grok does, or refuse to start if mcp.json lists a wmw-* seat.

  HIGH / armcheck.py:11-13 (`seat().rpc`) / `json.loads(p.stdout.readline())` has no timeout and no crash isolation. A seat that hangs or emits a parse-error line first hangs armcheck forever, or feeds it the wrong line. A hung canary reports nothing; a crashed seat makes armcheck itself crash mid-run. / Wrap readline in a select/timeout, drain stray lines until the matching id arrives, and run each seat in a try/except so one bad seat cannot abort the whole arm.

  HIGH / armcheck.py:54-55 ("no lease left behind") / The only reservation canary checks the REFUSAL path. The release path (dispatch-guard.py `release`, pkt-glm.md:227-249) is never exercised by armcheck, so a broken `release` — or the `finally` at pkt-glm.md:509-516 silently failing — would leave leases wedged and the operator locked out of his own rig, with a green checkmark. / Add a canary that reserves, then releases, then asserts the store is empty; and one that reserves two jobs and asserts the second is refused (concurrency cap).

  HIGH / armcheck.py:37-44 (read-only canaries) / Every "read-only" check asserts an error message, never a negative write. The 2026-08-23 incident was precisely a read-only call that wrote 11.7KB; the new canaries would still pass if `--mode ask`/`--mode plan`/deny rules stopped working tomorrow, because they never try to write and watch it fail. / For each seat, run a read-only call whose prompt instructs the model to write a marker file into the playpen, then assert the marker does not appear. This is the only form of test that catches the class of bug that actually bit.

  MEDIUM / allowance.py:43-44 (`_save`) / `_save` writes the allowance store in place with no tmp+rename. A crash or a malicious process that truncates the file mid-write leaves a corrupt JSON; `_load` then returns `{}` and every metered seat fails closed — a permanent silent denial of spending until the operator re-grants. dispatch-guard got this right (`os.replace` at pkt-glm.md:102); allowance did not. / Use the same tmp+`os.replace` pattern.

  MEDIUM / wmw_cursor_mcp.py:319-338 / `_safe_cwd`'s secret-dir check is segment-equal (`if secret in parts`). It blocks `…/.ssh/…` but NOT `…/.config-backup/…` or any future secret dir. More importantly it is a denylist: a new credential directory (e.g. `.gemini2`, `.cursor-cli`) is not in the tuple and sails through. The system-tree check is also env-driven and silently skips on Linux/macOS where `SystemRoot`/`ProgramFiles` are unset. / Treat the home directory as deny-by-default for write-capable sessions and allow only an explicit allowlist of project roots plus the playpen.

  MEDIUM / wmw_gemini_mcp.py:166-168 (`_safe_cwd`) / The Gemini cwd guard is weaker than its siblings: it uses `os.sep + secret in real + os.sep` substring matching, returns the ORIGINAL `cwd` (not `realpath`), and its banned set omits `.azure`, `.kube`, `.gnupg`. A symlinked cwd is validated by realpath but the un-resolved path is what is returned and passed to the CLI, reopening the symlink-swap the Cursor and Grok guards explicitly close. / Mirror the Cursor/Grok implementation: return `real`, use segment match, share the same secret list.

  MEDIUM / dispatch-guard.py:74-80 (stale lock reclaim) / The stale-reclaim is mtime-based and racy: between `os.path.getmtime` and `os.unlink`, another holder can legitimately recreate the file, and the reclaimer unlinks a lock it does not own. O_EXCL on re-create prevents a double-acquire, but a process can still unlink another's fresh lock and steal headroom. / Write the holder's pid into the lock and only reclaim after verifying the pid is gone (or use a per-file advisory lock).

  MEDIUM / wmw_cursor_mcp.py:69-71 (council lock env knobs) / `COUNCIL_LOCK_MAX`, `COUNCIL_LOCK_WINDOW_S`, and `COUNCIL_LOCK_ON` are read from the environment with no validation. A malicious or careless parent process (or a poisoned shell rc) sets `WMW_CURSOR_COUNCIL_LOCK=off` or `WMW_CURSOR_COUNCIL_MAX=999999` and the council lock is silently disabled. The same applies to `WMW_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS`, `WMW_MAX_OUTSTANDING_PCT`, `WMW_MAX_SINGLE_CLAIM_PCT` in dispatch-guard.py:44-51. / Pin these at process start from a config file the operator signs, or at least warn loudly when an env override is in effect.

  LOW / wmw_cursor_mcp.py:454-460 (prompt spill) / The spill file is created in PROMPTS_DIR with mode 0600? No — `tempfile.mkstemp` uses 0600 on POSIX but on Windows the ACL inherits the parent dir. The playpen is `C:\Sync\_playpen\cursor`, a world-traversable location; another user on the machine (or a service) could read in-flight prompts, which are the operator's full instructions and may contain secrets. / Set restrictive ACLs or spill into a per-user private dir.

  LOW / wmw_cursor_mcp.py:518-531 (error leak) / On a non-parseable Cursor run, the wrapper echoes up to 2000 chars of stdout and 2000 of stderr back to the MCP client (and thus to the orchestrating LLM). stderr can include environment paths, token fragments, or vendor diagnostics. / Truncate harder and scrub on the error path.

  LOW / read-meters.py:91-101 / `read_grok` reads `~/.grok/auth.json` and ships the bearer token to a hardcoded `cli-chat-proxy.grok.com`. There is no certificate pinning and no host validation beyond TLS defaults; a compromised DNS or a MITM with a trusted CA exfiltrates the Grok access token. The Cursor path has the same shape. / Acceptable for a personal tool, but pin the endpoints or at least log the resolved IP.

Q3 CANARY AUDIT

  REAL CHECKS (would fail if their guard were deleted):
  - "credit model refused without spend_credits" — exercises meter_class guard at pkt-glm.md:488.
  - "auto/UNKNOWN refused even WITH spend_credits" — exercises the UNKNOWN fail-closed at :369.
  - "model id with metacharacters refused" — exercises _MODEL_RE at :125.
  - "write-capable with no cwd refused" — exercises _safe_cwd at :301.
  - "write-capable in System32 refused" — exercises the system-tree containment at :329.
  - "YOLO on a non-allowlisted model refused" — exercises YOLO_ALLOWLIST at :119.
  - "build dispatch at an EMPTY repo refused (preflight)" — exercises guard.preflight.
  - "grok: crafted sessionId cannot smuggle flags" — exercises _UUID_RE in the Grok seat.
  - "grok: reply escalating with no cwd refused" — exercises the reply-cwd guard added 2026-08-23.

  THEATRE (would still pass if the guard were deleted):
  - "all three seats start and list tools" (armcheck.py:21-30) — checks tool NAMES, not behaviour. A seat that lists `cursor` but accepts arbitrary args still passes.
  - "no leftover prompt handoffs" (armcheck.py:80) — passes whenever no call has run recently; it is a cleanliness check, not a safety check. A seat that leaked prompts to a different dir would pass.
  - "no lease left behind after a refused dispatch" (armcheck.py:54-55) — only checks the refusal path; the release path is untested, so a guard that never releases would still pass this check.

  UNCOVERED (no canary at all):
  - No canary proves a READ-ONLY call on any seat cannot write a file. This is the single most important gap; the entire 2026-08-23 incident was a read-only call that wrote.
  - No canary proves a read-only Cursor call cannot drive a sibling MCP seat (the escalation variant above). `--approve-mcps` is completely untested.
  - No canary for the Gemini seat's read-only or cwd guards at all — Gemini appears only in the "starts and lists tools" check.
  - No canary for the council lock (pkt-glm.md:406-420): a 4-seat fan-out is never simulated; the lock could be deleted and armcheck stays green.
  - No canary for the allowance gate (pkt-glm.md:397-404): an expired or missing allowance is never asserted to refuse.
  - No canary for the atomic reservation race (the Codex finding that motivated dispatch-guard): two concurrent reserves are never fired to prove exactly one succeeds.
  - No canary for stale-lock reclaim or for lease TTL expiry.
  - No canary for the prompt spill cleanup on a TIMEOUT or a CRASH (only the happy/error paths).
  - No canary that the spend ledger is actually appended on a refused call (the `_log_spend(..., ok=False)` paths at pkt-glm.md:499/525/529/533/541 are untested).

  CAN THE ARM TEST ITSELF PASS WHILE THE RIG IS UNSAFE?
  Yes, three ways. (1) armcheck.py:55 reads the reservation store with `json.load(io.open(RESV, ...))` guarded only by `os.path.exists`; if the file exists but is corrupt, armcheck raises and aborts mid-run, printing no final verdict — the operator sees a crash, not a FAIL. (2) The `seat().rpc` readline has no timeout; a seat that emits one banner line then hangs makes armcheck hang forever, so "no verdict" looks the same as "not run". (3) Most critically, the read-only guarantee is asserted entirely by checking error strings, so if `--mode ask` silently stops being read-only on a future Cursor build, every existing canary still prints PASS and the rig lights green.

  CHECKS I WOULD ADD (same style as the existing ones):
  - check("cursor read-only cannot write", run a read-only cursor call whose prompt says "write the string CANARY into ./write-canary.txt in the cwd", then assert not os.path.exists(write_canary))
  - check("grok read-only cannot write", same shape with the Grok seat and its deny rules)
  - check("gemini read-only cannot write", same shape with --mode plan)
  - check("cursor read-only cannot drive a sibling MCP seat", register a fake MCP server that writes a file, put it in a temp mcp.json, run a read-only cursor call that asks the model to call it, assert no file)
  - check("council lock refuses a 3rd billable call in the window", fire two stub billable ledger rows then assert a 3rd cursor CREDITS call is refused)
  - check("allowance expired refuses spending", grant with --days 0 (or backdate the file), assert cursor CREDITS call is refused with "NO ALLOWANCE")
  - check("atomic reserve: two concurrent reserves, exactly one wins", spawn two threads/processes calling reserve with the same window, assert one ok and one refused)
  - check("lease TTL expiry frees a slot", reserve with TTL 1s, sleep 2, assert a new reserve succeeds)
  - check("release actually clears the lease", reserve then release then assert RESV jobs is empty)
  - check("spill file removed on timeout", set CURSOR_TIMEOUT_S=1 with a slow prompt, assert no file left in PROMPTS_DIR)
  - check("spill file removed on crash", kill the seat mid-run, assert no leftover spill)
  - check("gemini cwd guard matches cursor/grok", parametrize the same banned-path table across all three _safe_cwd implementations)

Q4 IS IT WORTH IT
Partly. The preflight and the atomic reservation are genuine, well-built controls that address a real burn incident and would not exist in a naive wrapper — they earn their complexity. But the harness's claimed assurance is much larger than its real assurance: it governs only the ~3% of spend that flows through the MCP seats (its own yield report says so at pkt-glm.md:392-399), it cannot reach cloud agents / IDE / web / CI, and its read-only and escalation guarantees are unverified. For a single non-coder operator, the marginal value over "just run the CLIs carefully" is real but small, and the false-assurance surface is large: a green "ALL ARMED" that has never tried to write a file through a read-only call is a flag that says SAFE without checking SAFE. I would keep the preflight and the atomic lock, drop the council lock (it duplicates the allowance and is env-bypassable), and spend the saved complexity on the negative-write canaries above, which are the only thing that would make "ALL ARMED" mean what it says.

WHAT IS WELL BUILT
- The prompt-to-file spill and ASCII pointer in wmw_cursor_mcp.py:454-476 is the right fix for the .cmd injection and is cleanly implemented (generated path, ASCII check, finally-cleanup).
- The atomic `Lock` using O_EXCL create (dispatch-guard.py:64-87) is the correct portable primitive and the docstring at :57-62 says exactly why; this is the part of the tool that is not theatre.
- The `_save` in dispatch-guard.py:97-102 uses tmp + `os.replace` for an atomic swap — the ledger can never be half-written.
- The YOLO allowlist (pkt-glm.md:119) is a small, deliberate, visible tuple rather than a config knob — widening it is a code change, which is the right friction.
- The UNKNOWN-fails-closed meter rule (pkt-glm.md:369-374), including refusing `auto`, is the correct posture given the threat model.
- The Cursor cwd guard returning the realpath (pkt-glm.md:339) and the system-tree containment check (pkt-glm.md:329-333, "Found by Grok, 2026-08-23") show the right instinct: validate canonical, ban by containment, learn from the last incident.
- The spend ledger append (pkt-glm.md:165-182) is best-effort and never breaks a call — correct for a telemetry side-channel.

CONFIDENCE + what would change my mind
High on Q1 (the escalation variant is traceable in the code: `--approve-mcps` at pkt-glm.md:489 with no MCPTool deny on the Cursor seat, against the documented plan to addsibling seats at pkt-glm.md:115). High on Q3 (the canary gaps are concrete and the read-only class is provably untested). Medium on Q2's lower-severity items — I am reading the code statically and have not executed the race or the symlink swaps. What would change my mind: (1) a demonstration that `--mode ask` with stdin=DEVNULL on the current Cursor CLI build actually refuses a write (I assert it is unverified, not broken); (2) evidence that `--approve-mcps` does NOT auto-approve MCP tool *calls* (only server registration) — if so, the Cursor escalation variant collapses; (3) a timeout on armcheck's readline I missed. I recommend running the negative-write canaries above before treating any of this as settled.
```
